title: Nankana left behind
hookLine: the new border left Guru Nanak's birthplace in Pakistan

lines: A REQUEST NEAR THE END OF THE ARDAS.
cards: Near the end of the Ardas, after the Gurus and the martyrs have been remembered, comes a request about places.
It asks God to grant the Khalsa open access to, and care of, the gurdwaras and holy places that were separated from the panth. Those few words carry a whole map.
When the border was drawn, the town where Guru Nanak was born, Nankana Sahib, fell on the Pakistan side. So did other places from his life.
People who had walked there for festivals now looked west at a line they couldn't freely cross.

teach.h: THE PLACE DIDN'T CHANGE. THE WAY DID.
teach.b: First, what was left. This path has already been to Nankana: the stories of Guru Nanak's birth and childhood, and earlier this year, the reformers who died to free its gurdwara.
Now a border runs between that town and the Sikhs of Indian Punjab. The place didn't change. The way to it did.

teach.h: THE ARDAS ASKS FOR OPEN ACCESS.
teach.b: The request for open access is said at the close of Sikh worship, in gurdwaras far from Punjab as well as in it. So the loss isn't kept in a museum. It's spoken, day after day, as a hope.
On special days, groups of Sikh pilgrims are given permission to cross and visit Nankana Sahib and other gurdwaras in Pakistan, and the Sikhs who live there and the people of the town receive them.
The way is narrow, but it isn't closed. Fourth, the longing.

In a hymn at Ang 96 of the Guru Granth Sahib, which tradition says he wrote while far from his Guru, Guru Arjan writes that his mind longs for the Guru's sight like the rain-bird crying out for the drop of rain.
The Sikh tradition already had words for missing a holy presence you can't reach, and those words fit a border too. In the Gurus' hymns, the One is not kept on one side of any line.
You can pray toward Nankana from anywhere.
Left behind: not forgotten, but asked for, and longed for.

games.q: you live in Amritsar. Guru Nanak's birthplace is now across a border you can't freely cross. what do Sikhs do?
o: let it go and stop speaking of it.
ask for open access in the Ardas, and cross with pilgrim groups when allowed.
build a copy at home and call it the same place.
games.why: the request is spoken at the close of Sikh worship, and on special days pilgrims cross. left behind, but not forgotten.

practice: If you know the direction, turn a little toward a place you can't visit: a grandparent's village, a house that was sold, a country you left, a grave far away, or Nankana itself.

Close your eyes and walk there in your mind, the road in, the door, the smell of the air; breathe in and arrive, breathe out and let the longing be there without fixing it. If you pray, Waheguru can be the word you carry in.

wordCard.voice: Nankana Sahib, Guru Nanak's birthplace, left on the Pakistan side of the new border, and remembered in the Ardas every day. Today's word.
